sections.heading: What the one public test at ten million shows
What the vendors report at ten million
Why ten million is hard in a way one million is not

slides.title: The ten-million-token *question*
slides.text: How big is the workload, and what has been shown at that size?

narration: The memory systems on the market are scored on conversations that would fit in a long email thread.
The work an enterprise wants remembered is measured in years of mail, chat, tickets and documents.
This page puts the two sizes side by side.
It shows what the only public test at that size gives every approach.
And it ends with the question the industry has not answered.

slides.caption: Memory systems are scored on conversations that fit in an email thread. The work an enterprise wants remembered is years of mail, chat, tickets and documents.

slides.title: What we will *cover*

narration: First, how large an enterprise memory workload is, in tokens, from sourced figures.
Then what the one public benchmark at ten million tokens shows.
Then what the vendors report at that size, and why the reports cannot be compared.
Then why ten million is hard in a way one million is not.
Last, the question itself, in three parts, left with you.

slides.caption: How large the workload is, in tokens. What the one public test at ten million shows. What the vendors report. Why ten million is hard. The question, left open.

slides.title: One worker, one *year*
slides.unit: tokens of received mail and chat per knowledge worker per year, derived
slides.text: Before attachments, documents, tickets or meetings.

narration: Start with one person.
Microsoft's Work Trend Index of June 2025 counts 117 emails received per weekday.
And 153 chat messages.
A public corpus of sent mail averages 144 words per message.
Take 250 working days and three quarters of a word per token.
Email alone is about 5.6 million tokens a year.
Add chat, at an assumed 20 words a message, and the total is 6 to 8 million.
That excludes attachments, documents, tickets and meetings.
The chat figure is an assumption, and the page says so.
Ten million tokens is a little more than one worker's year.

slides.caption: Microsoft counts 117 emails and 153 chat messages received per weekday. At 144 words per email, that is about 6 to 8 million tokens a year, derived.

slides.title: Sourced *anchors* for scale
head: Workload
Size

narration: Here are sourced anchors for the scale.
One public corpus holds the mail of about 150 senior staff at one company.
It is about half a million messages.
No token count is published; derived from message length it is roughly 100 million tokens.
A single enterprise mailbox quota is 100 gigabytes, with an archive of 1.5 terabytes.
A synthetic enterprise corpus built for retrieval research in 2026 holds about 500 thousand documents across nine source types.
Its authors say no real corpus of that size can be released.
All United States annual reports from 1993 to 2020 come to 6.5 billion tokens.
And English Wikipedia is 5.27 billion words.
A service desk, a claims team or an engineering programme needs a slice of the estate.
That slice starts at tens of millions of tokens and grows every day.
Ten million is the floor, not the ceiling.

slides.caption: One company's senior mail from the 2000s is about 100 million tokens. A mailbox quota is 100 gigabytes. All US annual reports since 1993 are 6.5 billion tokens.

slides.title: The one public test at *ten million*

narration: One public benchmark reaches ten million tokens.
It was published by two universities and accepted at a top conference in 2026.
It has one hundred synthetic conversations, twenty of them at 128 thousand tokens.
Then 35 at half a million, 35 at one million, and ten at ten million.
It has two thousand questions, two per ability per conversation.
The ten abilities are abstention, contradiction resolution, event ordering, information extraction and instruction following.
Then knowledge update, multi-session reasoning, preference following, summarisation and temporal reasoning.
A judge scores each answer against rubric points at 0, half, or 1.
The authors evaluated no commercial memory system.

slides.caption: BEAM has one hundred synthetic conversations, ten of them at ten million tokens, and two thousand questions across ten abilities. A judge scores each answer 0, 0.5 or 1.

slides.title: What the test *shows*
head: Length
Full context
Retrieval
Authors' memory
slides.text: Best backbone. Three other backbones score 0.19 to 0.24 at ten million.

narration: Here are the results for the best backbone, a one-million-token open-weight model.
Three approaches: full context, retrieval of the top five, and the authors' own memory design.
At 100 thousand tokens they score 0.24, 0.32 and 0.36.
At one million, 0.26, 0.31 and 0.34.
At ten million, 0.10, 0.25 and 0.27.
Three things stand out.
The scores are low at every length.
That includes 100 thousand tokens, a size the model reads in one call.
The memory design adds 6 to 11 points over retrieval, and no more.
And every method is strongest on abstention and weakest on contradiction resolution.

slides.caption: With a one-million-token model, full context scores 0.10 at ten million, retrieval 0.25, and the authors' memory design 0.27. Scores are low at every length.

slides.title: What the vendors *report*
head: Vendor
At 1M
At 10M
Conditions
rows: Own judge; settings differ by scale
slides.text: Vendor reported. Not comparable to the paper or to each other.

narration: Three vendors have published their own ten-million-token numbers.
The first reports 64.1 at one million and 48.6 at ten million.
Its documentation lists one hundred conversations per scale.
The released data has ten at ten million.
So the setup is unclear.
The second reports 0.67 at ten million.
It notes that its settings differ between scales: different conversations, models and retrieval procedures.
The third reports 0.631 at one million and 0.406 at ten million.
It adds that testing recall on data that fits a context window is no longer meaningful.
These rows are shown because they exist, not because they can be compared.
The scales differ, the judges differ, and the setups differ from the paper.
What they share is the shape: each falls from one million to ten million.
Each vendor chose to publish anyway. That is to their credit.

slides.caption: Three vendors published their own ten-million-token numbers. Each used its own judge and harness. None is comparable to the paper, and none has been reproduced.

slides.title: Two independent points *beside* them
slides.text: 11.1 against 1.2 at ten million; 72.5 against 48.5 at 115 million.

narration: Two independent data points sit beside the vendor rows.
A 2026 corpus benchmark reports a memory agent at 11.1 over ten million tokens.
Plain retrieval scores 1.2 on the same task.
A May 2026 benchmark goes past ten million, to 115 million tokens of agent trajectories.
Its best method stores the trajectories as files and searches them with a coding agent.
It scores 72.5 against 48.5 for retrieval.
That task is closer to an engineer's workspace than to a customer's history.

slides.caption: A 2026 corpus benchmark reports a memory agent at 11.1 and retrieval at 1.2 over ten million tokens. A 115-million-token benchmark reports a file-storing agent at 72.5.

slides.title: Why ten million is *hard*

narration: Why is ten million hard in a way one million is not?
Three separate mechanisms compound.
The first is arithmetic.
No shipped model reads ten million tokens in one call.
So every approach retrieves, and the retrieval is the whole game.
The second is the encoder.
An embedding separates a session about careers from one about cooking.
It does not separate one career message from twenty thousand others on the same topic.
At ten million tokens a single conversation holds about twenty thousand messages.
The third is spread.
The questions that fail worst need many messages from different points in a long history.
Event ordering, summarisation, and reasoning across sessions.
Find one message and stop, and you have found nothing useful.

slides.caption: Nothing can read the whole. The candidate pool is too dense for an encoder. And the evidence is spread across years. The three compound.

slides.title: At that density, *words* discriminate
slides.text: Word overlap predicts recall. Encoder choice does not.

narration: We measured the density problem ourselves, on one system, on the ten-million-token benchmark.
Exact word overlap between the question and the evidence predicts whether the evidence is found.
The choice of encoder does not.
This guide already keeps keyword search in the loop for names and identifiers.
At this density it stops being optional.
At this density it becomes the discriminating channel.
On those ten-million-token questions the gold evidence averages seven and a half messages.
It reaches 83.
This is why the 90 percent scores on the small benchmarks do not transfer.
Those benchmarks have pools of 28 to 48 sessions and mostly need one session per question.

slides.caption: On the ten-million-token benchmark, exact word overlap between question and evidence predicts whether the evidence is found. The choice of encoder does not.

slides.title: Question one: *which* architecture
slides.text: Useful recall over ten million tokens, at a bearable cost per question.

narration: This section does not recommend an architecture for enterprise scale.
No architecture has published a result that would justify one.
So the question is left with you, in three parts.
Part one.
Which architecture, if any, gives an agent useful recall over ten million tokens of an enterprise's own records?
And at a cost per question that a service desk or a claims team can bear?

slides.caption: Which architecture, if any, gives an agent useful recall over ten million tokens of its own records? And at a cost a service desk can bear?

slides.title: Question two: how would you *know*
slides.text: Independent, past the window, unit and judge stated, two tables.

narration: Part two.
How would you know?
The score would have to be independently produced.
On a corpus that does not fit a context window.
With the unit, the pool, the k and the judge stated.
And with retrieval-only and answered-question results in separate tables.
Nothing published so far meets all of that.

slides.caption: The score would have to be independently produced, on a corpus that does not fit a context window. Unit, pool, k and judge stated. Two separate tables.

slides.title: Question three: what would it *cost*
slides.text: Index once, or pay one to six hundred dollars per question.

narration: Part three.
What would it cost to index?
And how does that compare with sending everything to the model?
At list price that is between one dollar and six hundred dollars per ten million tokens, per question.
Until these three are answered, a memory system chosen for an enterprise workload is chosen on faith.
Our own research on the question is under way.
It will be published here when it is complete.

slides.caption: What would it cost to index? Sending everything to the model costs one to six hundred dollars per ten million tokens. How do the two compare?

slides.title: What to *remember*
items: Ten million is one worker's year

narration: Here is what to remember.
Ten million tokens is a little more than one worker's year of mail and chat.
It is the floor for an enterprise memory.
The best independent result at that size is 0.27 on a scale of 0 to 1.
The vendor numbers at that size are unchecked and cannot be compared.
The question is open, in three parts: which architecture, how would you know, and what would it cost.
The next page records the one measurement we have made ourselves.

slides.caption: Ten million tokens is one worker's year, and the floor. The best independent result there is 0.27. Vendor numbers are unchecked. The question is open.
